_: Live works chosen for the Hudson River School collection page, decided by a subagent on art-historical grounds, delegated by Charlie on 2026-09-23.
criteria: Landscape painting (including Cole's allegorical and imagined landscapes, and foreign scenery) made c. 1825 to 1880 by painters of the Hudson River School or commonly grouped with it, including second-generation and luminist painters; decided by painter and period, not by subject. Still lifes, wildlife pieces and post-1880 work are left out.

why.vl-0355: Albert Bierstadt, 1868: core second-generation painter; painted during his 1867 to 1869 European stay, and foreign scenery is part of the school's output (as with Church's tropics).
why.vl-0354: Albert Bierstadt, 1866: Yosemite, the school's signature Western subject.
why.vl-0358: John Frederick Kensett, 1854: White Mountains in autumn, a core school subject by a core painter.
why.vl-0461: Thomas Cole, 1828: the school's founder; a religious landscape of the founding years.
why.vl-0043: Frederic Edwin Church, 1847: Cole's only pupil, painted in the years right after his training.
why.vl-0046: William Stanley Haseltine, 1856: usually grouped with the school (luminist coasts); painted in Italy while training alongside Bierstadt and Whittredge.
why.vl-0045: Jasper F. Cropsey, 1870: core second-generation painter; the White Mountains.
why.vl-0465: Thomas Cole, 1828: companion to the Expulsion; founding-years religious landscape.
why.vl-0054: William Stanley Haseltine, 1869: kept with his 1856 work for consistency; painted after he settled in Rome in 1867, but the Mediterranean rock coasts are exactly the pictures that group him with the school.
why.vl-0297: Martin Johnson Heade, 1871: marsh landscape, the luminist strand of the school.
why.vl-0460: Thomas Cole, 1836: The Course of Empire, the school's best-known allegorical landscape series.
why.vl-0350: Albert Bierstadt, 1868: Sierra Nevada, his defining Western panorama type.
why.vl-0042: Robert S. Duncanson, 1867: recognized second-generation painter of the school; an imagined landscape after Moore's Lalla Rookh.
why.vl-0053: George Inness, 1866: before his Tonalist turn of the late 1870s; already Barbizon-leaning, but still within the period in which he is grouped with the school.
why.vl-0047: George Inness, 1858: early Inness, the phase usually counted with the school.
why.vl-0057: John Frederick Kensett, 1860s: Newport coast, his luminist shore subject.
why.vl-0466: Thomas Cole, 1842: The Voyage of Life, second of his two great allegorical series.
why.vl-0463: Thomas Cole, 1840: imagined architectural landscape; a canonical Cole, and the non-landscape exclusion is meant for still lifes, not for his allegories.
why.vl-0357: Sanford Robinson Gifford, 1868: Hudson River itself, luminist Gifford at his peak.
why.vl-0464: After Thomas Cole, c. 1863: an American copy of the period; Newfields says it was probably made from Smillie's engraving that the American Art-Union sent to its members in 1850, so it records how the school's images spread. Labeled as a copy.

borderline_excluded.vl-0291: Albert Bierstadt, 1884: after the c. 1880 end of the period, and a wildlife picture (bighorn sheep) more than a landscape.
borderline_excluded.vl-0216: Martin Johnson Heade, 1873: a flowering branch on a ledge; still life, not landscape.
borderline_excluded.vl-0356: Martin Johnson Heade, 1873: orchid with a hummingbird; has a jungle backdrop, but it is a botanical picture, so treated the same as Apple Blossoms.
